label: Riemannian Metrics
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 35 through 47 and installs the single object on which the whole subject rests: a smoothly varying inner product on tangent spaces. Everything later, lengths, angles, geodesics and curvature, is read off from this one structure, so we develop it carefully.

label: A Smoothly Varying Inner Product
notes: A Riemannian metric assigns to each point a positive definite symmetric bilinear form on the tangent space, and the assignment must vary differentiably with the point. Differentiability is the word that turns pointwise linear algebra into geometry on the whole manifold, so we stress it here.

label: The Metric in Local Coordinates
notes: In a chart the metric becomes a symmetric positive definite matrix of smooth functions, the components g of i and j. Reading the inner product of coordinate vector fields recovers these functions, and every computation in the chapter eventually reduces to manipulating this matrix.

label: Field of Metric Ellipses
notes: Picturing the unit ball of each inner product gives an ellipse at every point, and the way these ellipses stretch and tilt across the manifold is exactly the geometric content of the metric. A constant field is flat; a varying field encodes curvature to come.

label: Length of a Curve
notes: The speed of a curve at each instant is the metric norm of its velocity vector, and integrating that speed over the parameter interval defines the length. This integral is independent of reparametrization, so length is a genuine geometric quantity attached to the image curve.

label: Arc Length and Distance
notes: Arc length measured from a base point gives a preferred parameter in which the curve has unit speed. Taking the infimum of lengths over all curves joining two points defines the Riemannian distance, which turns a connected manifold into a metric space compatible with its topology.

label: Example: The Euclidean Metric
notes: On real n space the standard dot product, constant in every chart, is the model Riemannian metric. Its components form the identity matrix, lengths reduce to the familiar integral of the Euclidean speed, and every ellipse in the field is a round circle of the same radius.

label: Example: The Hyperbolic Half-Plane
notes: The Poincare upper half-plane carries the metric obtained by scaling the Euclidean form by one over y squared. Near the boundary distances blow up, so the field of ellipses shrinks downward; this single example already shows how varying metrics produce genuinely non-Euclidean geometry.

label: Induced Metric on a Submanifold
notes: An immersion pulls the ambient inner product back to the source, restricting it to tangent directions of the submanifold. A surface in three space inherits its first fundamental form this way, and the construction shows that submanifolds of any Riemannian manifold are themselves Riemannian.

label: Product Metrics
notes: On a product of two Riemannian manifolds the natural metric adds the two factor inner products on the splitting of the tangent space. The flat torus arises this way from a product of circles, and lengths of curves separate into contributions from each factor.

label: Isometries and Local Isometries
notes: A diffeomorphism is an isometry when its derivative preserves the inner product at every point, so it carries lengths, angles and distances unchanged. Dropping the global bijection requirement gives local isometries, the maps under which two manifolds are geometrically indistinguishable in the small.

label: Synthesis
notes: We now hold the metric, its coordinate matrix, the length and distance it defines, the canonical examples and the isometries that preserve it. These pieces are the working vocabulary for the affine connection and the covariant derivative that open the next chapter, so keep the ellipse picture in mind.
